Alexandria-Egypt.name: Alexandria
Alexandria-Egypt.evidence_basis: Founded 331 BC with ~920 ha walled intramural grid (Hanson 2016; Wilson 2011; Delia 1988); Diodorus 17.52 records 300,000 free inhabitants in 1st c. BC, peaking ~450k+ in 2nd c. AD before Aurelian's 272 AD sack and the 541 AD Justinianic Plague.

Ctesiphon-Iraq.name: Ctesiphon
Ctesiphon-Iraq.evidence_basis: Established in the 120s BC as Parthian winter capital opposite Seleucia (Strabo 16.1.16; Kröger 1993; Farrokh 2023) and expanded under the Sassanians into the >1,000 ha eastern al-Mada'in metropolitan conurbation (Adams 1965; Simpson 2015), peaking ~415k under Khosrow I-II.

Antioch-on-the-Orontes-Turkey.name: Antioch-on-the-Orontes
Antioch-on-the-Orontes-Turkey.evidence_basis: Founded 300 BC by Seleucus I (~600-650 ha walled including Epiphaneia and Orontes island; Downey 1961; Liebeschuetz 1972; Wilson 2011), peaking ~340k+ before Shapur I's 253/260 sacks, the 526 AD quake, 540 AD sack, and 542 AD plague.

Carthage-Tunisia.name: Carthage
Carthage-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Punic metropolis (~340 ha; Hoyos 2010; Wilson 2011) razed in 146 BC and refounded as Colonia Julia Carthago in 44/29 BC (~320 ha dense Roman grid; Hanson 2016), peaking ~300k+ under the Severans before Vandal/Byzantine contraction.

Seleucia-on-the-Tigris-Iraq.name: Seleucia-on-the-Tigris
Seleucia-on-the-Tigris-Iraq.evidence_basis: Founded c. 305 BC by Seleucus I (~550 ha walled Hippodamian grid; Adams 1965; Invernizzi 1993), peaking ~280k before Avidius Cassius' 165 AD and Severus' 198 AD sacks, then refounded c. 230 AD as circular Veh-Ardashir (~300 ha; Simpson 2015).

Ephesus-Turkey.name: Ephesus
Ephesus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Capital of Roman Asia (~345-415 ha Lysimachean wall circuit, ~245 ha core inhabited zone plus harbor suburbs; Groh 2006; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016), declining after the 262 AD Gothic sack, Cayster silting, and 6th c. plague.

Babylon-Iraq.name: Babylon
Babylon-Iraq.evidence_basis: Achaemenid imperial residence (~300 ha inhabited core inside ~900 ha Neo-Babylonian outer walls; Boiy 2004; Adams 1981), depopulated rapidly after Seleucus I transferred civic institutions to Seleucia in 275 BC.

Pergamon-Turkey.name: Pergamon
Pergamon-Turkey.evidence_basis: Attalid royal capital expanded across ~220 ha lower city in the Roman era (Radt 1999; Hanson 2016); Galen (De cogn. cur. animi 9.13) attests 40,000 adult male citizens in the 2nd c. AD, indicating ~125k-145k total inhabitants.

Smyrna-Turkey.name: Smyrna
Smyrna-Turkey.evidence_basis: Refounded on Mt. Pagos by Antigonus and Lysimachus (~195 ha Roman urban footprint; Cadoux 1938; Hanson 2016; Wilson 2011), rebuilt with imperial subsidy after the 178 AD earthquake.

Apamea-Syria.name: Apamea
Apamea-Syria.evidence_basis: Seleucid Tetrapolis military capital (~250-255 ha walled grid with 1.85 km colonnade; Balty 1981; Hanson 2016); Quirinius' 6/7 AD census records 117,000 free citizens in its civitas (~95k-110k urban peak), battered in Khosrow I's 573 AD sack.

Tarsus-Turkey.name: Tarsus
Tarsus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Capital of Cilicia on the Cydnus plain (~185 ha; Strabo 14.5.13; Goldman 1950; Hanson 2016), a major linen-weaving and philosophical center linking Anatolia to Syria via the Cilician Gates.

Bactra-Afghanistan.name: Bactra
Bactra-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Capital of Achaemenid, Greco-Bactrian, and Kushan Bactria (~800 ha outer oasis ramparts enclosing a >1 km diameter fortified Bala Hissar and lower city; Bernard 2005; Canepa 2020; Farrokh 2023), peaking ~85k under Kushan Silk Road prosperity.

Nicomedia-Turkey.name: Nicomedia
Nicomedia-Turkey.evidence_basis: Founded 264 BC by Nicomedes I of Bithynia (~160 ha; Foss 1996; Hanson 2016); Diocletian's eastern imperial capital (286-324 AD) peaking ~82k before Constantinople's rise and the catastrophic 358 AD earthquake.

Susa-Iran.name: Susa
Susa-Iran.evidence_basis: Achaemenid imperial residence and Seleucid-Parthian Greek polis (~100-120 ha core tells plus craft quarters; Wenke 1975; Boucharlat 1987/2009), rebuilt after Shapur II's 340s AD suppression as a Sassanid silk-weaving center.

Lepcis Magna-Libya.name: Lepcis Magna
Lepcis Magna-Libya.evidence_basis: Phoenician-Roman Tripolitanian metropolis (~130 ha dense Severan core inside ~420 ha outer circuit; Mattingly 1995; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016), peaking ~78k under Septimius Severus before 365 AD seismic and Austuriani shocks.

Sardis-Turkey.name: Sardis
Sardis-Turkey.evidence_basis: Achaemenid satrapal capital and Roman Lydian metropolis (~145 ha walled; Hanfmann 1983; Hanson 2016), rebuilt after the 17 AD quake and remaining populous until sacked during the 616 AD Sassanian invasion.

Memphis-Egypt.name: Memphis
Memphis-Egypt.evidence_basis: Achaemenid satrapal capital (~260 ha occupied tell/urban footprint; Thompson 2012; Tacoma 2006) gradually eclipsed by Ptolemaic-Roman Alexandria and shifting Nile channels, declining to a provincial bishopric by the 6th c. AD.

Jerusalem-Palestine.name: Jerusalem
Jerusalem-Palestine.evidence_basis: Walled area reached ~90-100 ha under Herod and Agrippa I (~60k-75k permanent residents; Broshi 1975; Geva 2014), devastated in 70 AD, refounded as Aelia Capitolina (130 AD), revived as Christian pilgrimage metropolis, and sacked by Sassanians in 614 AD.

Istakhr-Iran.name: Istakhr
Istakhr-Iran.evidence_basis: Successor to Persepolis as Frataraka and Sassanid ancestral capital in Fars (~80 ha walled core plus extensive Marvdasht suburban complex; Whitcomb 1979; Callieri 2014), sustaining ~60k-68k inhabitants through the Sassanid era.

Gundeshapur-Iran.name: Gundeshapur
Gundeshapur-Iran.evidence_basis: Founded c. 271 AD by Shapur I using deported Roman craftsmen (~250-300 ha rectangular chessboard grid; Adams & Hansen 1968; Potts 1989), growing into Khuzestan's premier royal residence and medical-academic metropolis.

Damascus-Syria.name: Damascus
Damascus-Syria.evidence_basis: Ghouta oasis metropolis laid out on a ~135 ha Hellenistic-Roman grid (Burns 2005; Sartre 2005; Hanson 2016), maintaining high demographic resilience into Late Antiquity as a Ghassanid-Byzantine border hub.

Rhagae-Iran.name: Rhagae
Rhagae-Iran.evidence_basis: Tripartite Median-Parthian-Sassanid metropolis (15 ha fortified sharestan + 3.6 ha kohandezh + >200 ha savad suburbs; Rante 2008/2015; Farrokh 2023), seat of the Mihran noble house and prime Silk Road node.

Palmyra-Syria.name: Palmyra
Palmyra-Syria.evidence_basis: Syrian Desert caravan oasis metropolis (~120 ha walled core; Gawlikowski 1994; Hanson 2016) peaking ~60k-65k under the caravan boom and Zenobia before catastrophic reduction following Aurelian's 273 AD sack.

Artaxata-Armenia.name: Artaxata
Artaxata-Armenia.evidence_basis: Founded 176 BC by Artaxias I across nine fortified hills on the Aras (~350-400 ha sprawling urban hills and riverine suburbs; Khachatryan 1981; Lichtenberger & Zardaryan 2021), rebuilt after Corbulo's 58 AD sack and eclipsed by Dvin after Shapur II's 368 AD devastation.

Cyzicus-Turkey.name: Cyzicus
Cyzicus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Wealthy Propontis commercial metropolis and Hellespontus capital (~140 ha isthmus with Hadrianic temple and amphitheater; Hasluck 1910; Hanson 2016), severely damaged by the 543 AD earthquake.

Ecbatana-Iran.name: Ecbatana
Ecbatana-Iran.evidence_basis: Achaemenid, Seleucid, and Parthian royal summer capital (~150+ ha including Hagmatana and Mosalla citadels; Brown 1997; Boucharlat 2014; Farrokh 2023) controlling the Royal Road across the Zagros.

Caesarea Maritima-Israel.name: Caesarea Maritima
Caesarea Maritima-Israel.evidence_basis: Built 22-10 BC by Herod the Great with artificial harbor Sebastos (~45 ha Herodian core expanding to ~135 ha Late Roman walled circuit; Holum et al. 1988; Hanson 2016), serving as Roman/Byzantine capital of Palaestina Prima.

Cyrene-Libya.name: Cyrene
Cyrene-Libya.evidence_basis: Greek Pentapolis metropolis (~115-123 ha intramural; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016) prospering on silphium and grain exports until devastated by the 115-117 AD Kitos War revolt and the 262 and 365 AD earthquakes.

Salamis Cyprus-Cyprus.name: Salamis Cyprus
Salamis Cyprus-Cyprus.evidence_basis: Premier commercial polis of Cyprus (~165 ha urban sprawl with 15,000-seat theater and gymnasium; Karageorghis 1969; Hanson 2016); hit by the 116 AD revolt and 332/342 AD quakes, then rebuilt by Constantius II as island capital Constantia.

Tyre-Lebanon.name: Tyre
Tyre-Lebanon.evidence_basis: Phoenician-Roman purple-dye and glassmaking metropolis (~120 ha causewayed island plus Palaetyrus mainland; Rey-Coquais 1979; Hanson 2016), rebounding strongly after Alexander's 332 BC siege to serve as capital of Syria Phoenice.

Edessa-Turkey.name: Edessa
Edessa-Turkey.evidence_basis: Capital of the Abgarid Kingdom of Osrhoene and Roman Mesopotamia (~120 ha intramural; Segal 1970; Ross 2001), flourishing as the leading Syriac Christian intellectual and frontier commercial metropolis.

Hadrumetum-Tunisia.name: Hadrumetum
Hadrumetum-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Major Punic-Roman grain and olive-oil export harbor (~155 ha walled footprint; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016), elevated to capital of Valeria Byzacena under Diocletian and refortified by Justinian.

Dvin-Armenia.name: Dvin
Dvin-Armenia.evidence_basis: Founded c. 335 AD by Khosrov III Kotak (~320 ha citadel and fortified lower city; Kalantaryan 1996), succeeding Artaxata as seat of the Sassanid marzpan and Armenian Catholicos on the Aras trade trunk.

Ancyra-Turkey.name: Ancyra
Ancyra-Turkey.evidence_basis: Galatian Tectosages tribal center made capital of Roman Galatia in 25 BC (~125 ha; Mitchell 1993; Hanson 2016), anchoring the Anatolian highway network until the 622 AD Persian raid.

Nicaea-Turkey.name: Nicaea
Nicaea-Turkey.evidence_basis: Hellenistic foundation of Antigonus and Lysimachus (~130 ha enclosed by 5 km Roman-Late Antique walls; Foss 1996; Hanson 2016), hosting the First Ecumenical Council (325 AD).

Charax Spasinu-Iraq.name: Charax Spasinu
Charax Spasinu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Founded 324 BC by Alexander and refounded by Hyspaosines (~280 ha mapped intramural grid at Jebel Khayaber; Campbell et al. 2019; Gregoratti 2011), flourishing as Persian Gulf entrepot for Palmyrene and Indian trade before late Sassanian silting.

Sais-Egypt.name: Sais
Sais-Egypt.evidence_basis: Twenty-Sixth Dynasty royal capital until the 525 BC Persian conquest (~140 ha enclosure; Wilson 2006; Tacoma 2006), contracting steadily into a regional Western Delta nome metropolis under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

Hatra-Iraq.name: Hatra
Hatra-Iraq.evidence_basis: Parthian-allied Arab kingdom capital enclosed by ~320 ha double circular walls around a 435x320 m central temenos (Sommer 2003; Foietta 2015; Farrokh 2023), repelling Trajan and Severus before total destruction by Shapur I in 240-241 AD.

Nishapur-Iran.name: Nishapur
Nishapur-Iran.evidence_basis: Founded mid-3rd c. AD by Shapur I as administrative capital of Abarshahr/Khorasan (~150+ ha Sassanid core beneath Tepe Alp Arslan/Shadyakh; Bulliet 1972; Rante & Collinet 2013), rising steadily into late antiquity.

Kapisa-Afghanistan.name: Kapisa
Kapisa-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Kushan summer capital at the Panjshir-Ghorband confluence (~80 ha fortified urban complex yielding the Roman-Indian-Chinese Begram Hoard; Ghirshman 1946; Mehendale 2001), raided c. 241 AD by Shapur I and still thriving when Xuanzang visited c. 630 AD.

Caesarea Mazaca-Turkey.name: Caesarea Mazaca
Caesarea Mazaca-Turkey.evidence_basis: Cappadocian royal seat and Roman provincial capital (~115 ha; Mitchell 1993; Hanson 2016), suffering heavy deportation in Shapur I's 260 AD sack before recovering under Basil of Caesarea.

Bishapur-Iran.name: Bishapur
Bishapur-Iran.evidence_basis: Planned royal city founded 266 AD by Shapur I (~150-185 ha orthogonal walled grid with Greco-Roman mosaic palace and Anahita temple; Ghirshman 1956-1971), housing ~45k-50k at its Sassanid peak.

Miletus-Turkey.name: Miletus
Miletus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Ionian Hippodamian grid city (~100 ha peninsula; Greaves 2002; Hanson 2016) recovering after the 494 BC Persian sack and 334 BC siege before long-term Maeander alluviation choked its four harbors.

Caesarea Mauretaniae-Algeria.name: Caesarea Mauretaniae
Caesarea Mauretaniae-Algeria.evidence_basis: Punic Iol refounded by Juba II (25 BC) as royal and later Roman provincial capital (~318-370 ha walled perimeter with ~150 ha dense built-up core; Leveau 1984; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016), sacked during Firmus' revolt in 371 AD.

Berytus-Lebanon.name: Berytus
Berytus-Lebanon.evidence_basis: Elevated to Colonia Julia Augusta Felix Berytus in 15 BC (~95 ha; Hall 2004; Hanson 2016), booming as the Roman East's premier law-school metropolis until shattered by the catastrophic 551 AD earthquake and tsunami.

Nisibis-Turkey.name: Nisibis
Nisibis-Turkey.evidence_basis: Strategic Upper Mesopotamian fortress-city (~110 ha walled; Lightfoot 1988; Farrokh 2023), serving as the chief Roman-Sassanian border customs depot and Syriac academy hub after its 363 AD cession to Persia.

Tigranocerta-Turkey.name: Tigranocerta
Tigranocerta-Turkey.evidence_basis: Founded c. 77 BC by Tigranes the Great with deported Anatolian populations (Plutarch Lucullus 26; Sinclair 1994), sacked by Lucullus in 69 BC and later refortified by Theodosius II and Justinian as Byzantine Martyropolis.

Laodicea on the Lycus-Turkey.name: Laodicea on the Lycus
Laodicea on the Lycus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Founded c. 261 BC by Antiochus II (~120 ha plateau with twin theaters and stadium; Simsek 2013; Hanson 2016), enriched by Phrygian black-wool trade before the devastating 494 AD earthquake.

Alexandria in Aria-Afghanistan.name: Alexandria in Aria
Alexandria in Aria-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Hari Rud oasis metropolis and Alexandrian citadel (~130 ha fortified core; Vogelsang 2002; Farrokh 2023), serving continuously as a strategic Parthian, Kushano-Sasanian, and Sassanid western Afghan hub.

Emesa-Syria.name: Emesa
Emesa-Syria.evidence_basis: Arab Emesene royal seat and capital of Syria Phoenice Libanensis (~110 ha; Sartre 2005; Hanson 2016), rising under Severan patronage as a major Orontes agricultural and textile center.

Amida-Turkey.name: Amida
Amida-Turkey.evidence_basis: Upper Tigris basalt fortress-city greatly expanded and fortified by Constantius II in 349 AD (~145 ha walled; Gabriel 1940; Crow 2007), absorbing refugees from Nisibis before heavy losses in Kavad I's 503 AD sack.

Hecatompylos-Iran.name: Hecatompylos
Hecatompylos-Iran.evidence_basis: Early Arsacid Parthian royal capital in Qumis (dispersed elite compounds and settlement clusters across ~2,800 ha alluvial plain; Hansman 1968; Farrokh 2023), declining after capital relocation to Ctesiphon and rise of Damghan.

Arsinoe-Egypt.name: Arsinoe
Arsinoe-Egypt.evidence_basis: Fayum nome metropolis expanded by Ptolemaic land reclamation (~190 ha; Bagnall & Frier 1994; Tacoma 2006); surviving Roman census returns and 2nd c. AD water-supply/poll-tax registers indicate ~40k-44k peak residents.

Arbela-Iraq.name: Arbela
Arbela-Iraq.evidence_basis: Capital of the Parthian-Sassanid client kingdom and metropolitan bishopric of Adiabene (~100 ha citadel tell plus lower town; Novácek et al. 2013), sustaining stable urban continuity across classical antiquity.

Cirta-Algeria.name: Cirta
Cirta-Algeria.evidence_basis: Numidian royal capital of Massinissa and Micipsa and later Roman confederation capital (~110 ha plateau and lower terraces; Berthier 1981; Hanson 2016), rebuilt by Constantine after 311 AD civil war damage.

Gor-Iran.name: Gor
Gor-Iran.evidence_basis: Foundational circular capital built c. 220 AD by Ardashir I (~300 ha inside 1.95 km diameter radial ramparts; Huff 1974-2008; Farrokh 2023), serving as the administrative seat of Ardashir-Khwarrah province.

Jayy-Iran.name: Jayy
Jayy-Iran.evidence_basis: Circular Sassanid military muster city and administrative core of Spahan alongside twin suburb Yahudiyya (~120 ha walled circular enclosure; Golombek 1974; Kamaly 2006).

Utica-Tunisia.name: Utica
Utica-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Phoenician port (~95 ha walled; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016) serving as provincial capital of Roman Africa from 146 BC until Carthage's Augustan revival, later declining due to Medjerda delta alluviation.

Hermopolis Magna-Egypt.name: Hermopolis Magna
Hermopolis Magna-Egypt.evidence_basis: Middle Egypt nome capital (~120 ha; Bagnall & Frier 1994; Tacoma 2006); mid-3rd c. AD urban house register documenting ~7,000 houses across four quarters implies ~37k-43k inhabitants at peak.

Partaw-Azerbaijan.name: Partaw
Partaw-Azerbaijan.evidence_basis: Founded/refortified under Sassanian King Peroz I (459-484 AD) as the new capital of Caucasian Albania (~200+ ha earthwork perimeter; Trever 1959; Wordsworth 2018), rapidly surpassing Qabala as the Kura valley metropolis.

Thysdrus-Tunisia.name: Thysdrus
Thysdrus-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Sahel olive-oil boomtown (~120 ha urban grid with 35,000-seat amphitheater; Slim 1990; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016) peaking ~38k before severe devastation during the 238 AD suppression of the Gordian revolt.

Gaza-Palestine.name: Gaza
Gaza-Palestine.evidence_basis: Mediterranean terminus of the Nabataean frankincense trail (~90 ha plus port Maiumas; Glucker 1987; Hanson 2016), surging in 4th-6th c. wine-export prosperity and renowned rhetorical schools.

Al-Hira-Iraq.name: Al-Hira
Al-Hira-Iraq.evidence_basis: Capital of the Lakhmid Arab kingdom on the lower Euphrates desert margin (~160 ha dispersed qasr, monastic, and residential quarters; Toral-Niehoff 2014; Simpson 2015), peaking ~38k before Lakhmid dissolution in 602 AD.

Sidon-Lebanon.name: Sidon
Sidon-Lebanon.evidence_basis: Major Phoenician naval and glass-blowing port (~85 ha; Jidejian 1971; Hanson 2016) recovering after Artaxerxes III's 351 BC sack and damaged by the 551 AD coastal earthquake-tsunami.

Bostra-Syria.name: Bostra
Bostra-Syria.evidence_basis: Northern Nabataean royal seat made capital of Roman Arabia Petraea and base of Legio III Cyrenaica in 106 AD (~95 ha with 15,000-seat theater; Sartre 1985; Hanson 2016).

Scythopolis-Israel.name: Scythopolis
Scythopolis-Israel.evidence_basis: Largest Decapolis city and Late Antique capital of Palaestina Secunda (~115-130 ha expanded Byzantine walls; Tsafrir & Foerster 1997; Hanson 2016) renowned for its fine linen industry.

Halicarnassus-Turkey.name: Halicarnassus
Halicarnassus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Carian satrapal capital expanded via Mausolus' synoecism (~130 ha circuit; Pedersen 2010; Hanson 2016), battered during Alexander's 334 BC siege before stabilizing as a prosperous Roman port.

Beroea-Syria.name: Beroea
Beroea-Syria.evidence_basis: Ancient Halab refounded by Seleucus I on a ~95 ha orthogonal grid beneath its citadel (Sauvaget 1941; Hanson 2016), remaining a busy northern Syrian market town despite Khosrow I's 540 AD sack.

Alexandria in Arachosia-Afghanistan.name: Alexandria in Arachosia
Alexandria in Arachosia-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Achaemenid-Alexandrian-Mauryan-Kushan fortified city (~100 ha enclosed ramparts around a 30 m high citadel platform with Ashokan Greek/Aramaic edicts; McNicoll & Ball 1996; Helms 1997; Farrokh 2023).

Oxyrhynchus-Egypt.name: Oxyrhynchus
Oxyrhynchus-Egypt.evidence_basis: Metropolis of the Oxyrhynchite nome (~110 ha; Bagnall & Frier 1994; Tacoma 2006); 3rd c. AD grain-dole archive (4,000 adult male recipients) and ~11,000-seat theater point to ~30k-36k residents.

Shushtar-Iran.name: Shushtar
Shushtar-Iran.evidence_basis: Khuzestan hydraulic-engineering metropolis (~80 ha; Adams 1962; Potts 1999) transformed by Shapur I's Roman-built Band-e Kaisar bridge-weir and irrigation canals supporting silk and sugar cultivation.

Ma'rib-Yemen.name: Ma'rib
Ma'rib-Yemen.evidence_basis: Largest ancient South Arabian walled city (~98 ha intramural sustained by the 9,600 ha Ma'rib Dam oasis; Brunner 1997; Vogt 2004 ~25k-35k), collapsing demographically after final dam failure c. 570-575 AD.

Ptolemais Cyrenaica-Libya.name: Ptolemais Cyrenaica
Ptolemais Cyrenaica-Libya.evidence_basis: Founded mid-3rd c. BC by Ptolemy III (~217 ha walled circuit containing substantial open garden/cistern plots; Kraeling 1962; Wilson 2011); elevated to capital of Libya Pentapolis under Diocletian before 5th c. aqueduct collapse.

Sinope-Turkey.name: Sinope
Sinope-Turkey.evidence_basis: Milesian colony, royal capital of Mithridates VI of Pontus, and Caesarian Roman colonia (~65 ha fortified peninsula; Doonan 2004; Hanson 2016) dominating Black Sea amphora and olive-oil trade.

Vagharshapat-Armenia.name: Vagharshapat
Vagharshapat-Armenia.evidence_basis: Arshakuni royal capital rebuilt by Vologases I c. 120-140 AD (~110 ha walled Ararat plain city; Hewsen 2001), becoming the ecclesiastical mother see of Armenia after Gregory the Illuminator's c. 301 AD foundation.

Zeugma-Turkey.name: Zeugma
Zeugma-Turkey.evidence_basis: Founded c. 300 BC by Seleucus I as twin Euphrates bridgehead and garrison of Legio IV Scythica (~90 ha terraced villas; Kennedy 1998; Görkay 2015; Hanson 2016), never fully recovering after Shapur I's 253 AD sack.

Antinoopolis-Egypt.name: Antinoopolis
Antinoopolis-Egypt.evidence_basis: Founded 130 AD by Hadrian as a privileged Greek polis (~135 ha orthogonal grid; Hanson 2016; Tacoma 2006), later elevated to capital of the Thebaid province under Diocletian.

Nagarahara-Afghanistan.name: Nagarahara
Nagarahara-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Gandharan-Kushan Buddhist pilgrimage and Kabul River valley trade center (~80 ha urban and stupa-monastery complex at Hadda; Tarzi 1990; Ball 2019), declining after 5th-6th c. Hephthalite disruptions.

Side-Turkey.name: Side
Side-Turkey.evidence_basis: Pamphylian harbor metropolis (~55 ha peninsula with 15,000-seat theater and major aqueduct; Mansel 1963; Hanson 2016) flourishing in Roman and 5th-6th c. Byzantine commerce.

Samosata-Turkey.name: Samosata
Samosata-Turkey.evidence_basis: Royal capital of Commagene and Roman Euphrates legionary base of Legio XVI Flavia Firma (~85 ha walled city and acropolis tell; Özgüç 2009; Hanson 2016).

Darabgird-Iran.name: Darabgird
Darabgird-Iran.evidence_basis: Circular Parthian-Sassanid provincial capital of eastern Fars (~235 ha enclosed within massive earthen ramparts and ditch; Huff 1994; Morgan 2003), minting Sassanid coinage continuously.

Ai-Khanoum-Afghanistan.name: Ai-Khanoum
Ai-Khanoum-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Greco-Bactrian royal foundation at the Oxus-Kokcha confluence (~180-200 ha walled triangle with 5,000-seat theater, gymnasium, and palace; Bernard 1982; Martinez-Sève 2014; Farrokh 2023), sacked and abandoned c. 145 BC.

Mtskheta-Georgia.name: Mtskheta
Mtskheta-Georgia.evidence_basis: Capital of the Kingdom of Iberia at the Kura-Aragvi confluence (~90 ha Armaztsikhe citadel, Sarkine, and riverside quarters; Apakidze 1968; Braund 1994), gradually yielding secular primacy to Tbilisi after c. 458 AD.

Tanis-Egypt.name: Tanis
Tanis-Egypt.evidence_basis: Major Eastern Delta nome capital (~115 ha tell complex; Brissaud 1996; Tacoma 2006) retaining substantial Ptolemaic temple and residential sectors before progressive Tanitic branch silting in Late Antiquity.

Petra-Jordan.name: Petra
Petra-Jordan.evidence_basis: Nabataean royal capital (~40 ha dense civic core plus suburban basin quarters and 8,000-seat theater; Fiema 2002; Graf 2007 ~25k-35k peak), declining after Roman annexation (106 AD), trade rerouting, and the 363 and 551 AD earthquakes.

Veh-Ardashir Kerman-Iran.name: Veh-Ardashir Kerman
Veh-Ardashir Kerman-Iran.evidence_basis: Founded by Ardashir I c. 230 AD as Sassanid provincial capital of Kirman (~85 ha walled oasis town; Brunner 1983), anchoring southeastern plateau trade routes toward Sistan and Hormuz.

Pelusium-Egypt.name: Pelusium
Pelusium-Egypt.evidence_basis: Eastern Delta fortress-port and capital of Augustamnica Prima (~95 ha including theater and citadel; Hanson 2016; Abd el-Maqsoud 1998), hit catastrophically as the 541 AD entry point of the Justinianic Plague.

Perge-Turkey.name: Perge
Perge-Turkey.evidence_basis: Pamphylian metropolis (~60 ha fortified city plus extramural stadium and theater for 12,000; Abbasoglu 2001; Hanson 2016) flourishing under Flavian-Severan benefactors.

Zaranj-Afghanistan.name: Zaranj
Zaranj-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Ancient capital of Drangiana and Sassanid Sakastan in the irrigated Helmand-Sistan delta (~90 ha fortified core at Nad-i Ali / Zarang; Dales 1977; Bosworth 1968), sustaining ~25k-29k inhabitants.

Ptolemais Hermiou-Egypt.name: Ptolemais Hermiou
Ptolemais Hermiou-Egypt.evidence_basis: Founded c. 300 BC by Ptolemy I Soter as the autonomous Greek polis of Upper Egypt (~100 ha; Strabo 17.1.42; Tacoma 2006), serving as the chief Hellenic administrative center of the Thebaid until eclipsed by Antinoopolis.

Sanaa-Yemen.name: Sanaa
Sanaa-Yemen.evidence_basis: Highland Sabaean-Himyarite fortress town of Ghumdan Palace elevated to Yemen's capital under Aksumite viceroy Abraha (530s AD) and Sassanian governor Wahriz (570 AD; Robin 2012).

Oea-Libya.name: Oea
Oea-Libya.evidence_basis: Tripolitanian emporium (~68 ha walled peninsula; Mattingly 1995; Hanson 2016) that weathered late antique crisis better than Lepcis and Sabratha, surviving as the primary port of Tripolitania.

Ashkelon-Israel.name: Ashkelon
Ashkelon-Israel.evidence_basis: Autonomous Hellenistic-Roman coastal polis (~65 ha fortified tell; Stager et al. 2008; Hanson 2016) sustaining high-volume amphora wine exports through the Byzantine period.

Hippo Regius-Algeria.name: Hippo Regius
Hippo Regius-Algeria.evidence_basis: Coastal Numidian royal seat and Roman grain-exporting port (~60-65 ha; Marec 1954; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016), episcopal seat of Augustine until the 430-431 AD Vandal siege.

Kunduz-Afghanistan.name: Kunduz
Kunduz-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Eastern Bactrian irrigated plain fortress-town (~75 ha Bala Hissar and surrounding urban oasis; Ball 2019) serving as the Hephthalite and Western Turk administrative center of Tokharistan.

Zafar-Yemen.name: Zafar
Zafar-Yemen.evidence_basis: Highland capital of the Himyarite Kingdom (~110 ha fortified twin volcanic hills; Yule 2007/2013 ~20k-30k peak), declining abruptly after the 525 AD Aksumite conquest and transfer of royal administration to Sanaa.

Qabala-Azerbaijan.name: Qabala
Qabala-Azerbaijan.evidence_basis: Ancient capital of Caucasian Albania attested by Pliny NH 6.29 (~150+ ha Salbir and Gala fortified sectors; Babaev 1990), flourishing until political primacy shifted south to Partaw in the late 5th c. AD.

Carrhae-Turkey.name: Carrhae
Carrhae-Turkey.evidence_basis: Macedonian veteran colony and Roman municipium on the Balikh plain (~90 ha walled circuit; Rice 1952; Segal 1970), enduring as a prominent moon-cult sanctuary and caravan crossroads.

Sabratha-Libya.name: Sabratha
Sabratha-Libya.evidence_basis: Western Tripolitanian trading port (~58 ha with 5,000-seat theater; Kenrick 1986; Mattingly 1995; Wilson 2011), heavily damaged by the 365 AD earthquake and reduced to a fortified Byzantine enclave.

Lambaesis-Algeria.name: Lambaesis
Lambaesis-Algeria.evidence_basis: Headquarters of Legio III Augusta and capital of Roman Numidia (~85 ha fortress plus canabae municipium; Janon 1973; Hanson 2016), declining after Diocletian shifted administrative primacy back to Cirta.

Philadelphia-Jordan.name: Philadelphia
Philadelphia-Jordan.evidence_basis: Ammonite capital refounded by Ptolemy II Philadelphus (~70 ha citadel and wadi floor with 6,000-seat theater; Northedge 1992; Hanson 2016) anchoring the Via Nova Traiana.

Tiberias-Israel.name: Tiberias
Tiberias-Israel.evidence_basis: Founded c. 20 AD by Herod Antipas on the Sea of Galilee (~55 ha including Hammat thermal suburb; Hirschfeld 2004; Hanson 2016), becoming the chief rabbinic academy center of Late Antique Galilee.

Tbilisi-Georgia.name: Tbilisi
Tbilisi-Georgia.evidence_basis: Founded c. 458 AD by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali around sulfur springs and Narikala gorge fortifications (Suny 1994; Braund 1994), rising as Iberia's capital before the 627-628 AD Byzantine-Khazar siege.

Trapezus-Turkey.name: Trapezus
Trapezus-Turkey.evidence_basis: Eastern Black Sea Greek polis and headquarters of the Roman Classis Pontica (~50 ha; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Hanson 2016), sacked by Goths in 257 AD and rebuilt by Justinian as a supply base for the Persian wars.

Tingis-Morocco.name: Tingis
Tingis-Morocco.evidence_basis: Phoenician-Mauretanian strait port and provincial capital of Mauretania Tingitana (~55 ha; Ponsich 1970; Hanson 2016), retaining maritime strategic importance into the Byzantine period.

Aphrodisias-Turkey.name: Aphrodisias
Aphrodisias-Turkey.evidence_basis: Carian free city and later provincial capital of Caria (~90 ha within 3.5 km walls, ~30,000-seat stadium; Ratté 2001; Hanson 2016), famed for its imperial marble-sculpting industry.

Yathrib-Saudi Arabia.name: Yathrib
Yathrib-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Fertile volcanic-plain date-palm oasis organized into fortified clan settlements (atum) of Aws, Khazraj, and Jewish tribes (Watt 1956; Lecker 1995), surging after the 622 AD Hijra as capital of the early Islamic umma.

Coptos-Egypt.name: Coptos
Coptos-Egypt.evidence_basis: Upper Egyptian Nile terminus of Eastern Desert caravan tracks to Berenike and Myos Hormos (~60 ha; Sidebotham 2011; Tacoma 2006), booming under early Roman Indian Ocean trade before Diocletian's 292 AD sack.

Berenice Cyrenaica-Libya.name: Berenice Cyrenaica
Berenice Cyrenaica-Libya.evidence_basis: Westernmost Pentapolis port transferred from Euesperides c. 246 BC (~65 ha; Lloyd 1977; Hanson 2016) with active Mediterranean commerce and surviving Justinianic walls.

Najran-Saudi Arabia.name: Najran
Najran-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Major incense-route oasis bifurcating Hijazi and Gulf caravan tracks (~65 ha walled Al-Ukhdud core plus oasis settlements; Robin 2010), renowned as South Arabia's chief 5th-6th c. Christian bishopric.

Sepphoris-Israel.name: Sepphoris
Sepphoris-Israel.evidence_basis: Galilean capital rebuilt by Herod Antipas (~60 ha ridge and lower plateau with 4,500-seat theater; Meyers & Chancey 2012; Hanson 2016), seat of the Sanhedrin until damaged in the 363 AD Galilee earthquake.

Gerasa-Jordan.name: Gerasa
Gerasa-Jordan.evidence_basis: Decapolis polis (~85 ha intramural with oval plaza, colonnaded cardo, and two theaters; Kraeling 1938; Kennedy 2007; Hanson 2016 ~15k-22k) experiencing a vigorous 6th c. Christian basilica-building boom.

Ghazni-Afghanistan.name: Ghazni
Ghazni-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Highland Zabulistan commercial and Buddhist center on the Kandahar-Kabul road (~55 ha including Tepe Sardar monastic suburb; Taddei 1968; Ball 2019), thriving under Kidarite and Nezak rulers.

Tipasa-Algeria.name: Tipasa
Tipasa-Algeria.evidence_basis: Punic trading post elevated to Roman colonia in Mauretania Caesariensis (~70 ha walled circuit with amphitheater and basilicas; Lancel 1982; Hanson 2016), contracting after 484 AD Vandal persecution.

Kition-Cyprus.name: Kition
Kition-Cyprus.evidence_basis: Phoenician-Cypriot harbor kingdom absorbed by the Ptolemies in 312 BC (~50 ha; Yon 2006; Hanson 2016), maintaining steady maritime salt and copper trade under Roman and Byzantine rule.

Bamiyan-Afghanistan.name: Bamiyan
Bamiyan-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Hindu Kush Silk Road pass principality and colossal Buddhist cave-monastery valley (Tarzi 1977; Klimburg-Salter 1989); Xuanzang (c. 630 AD) records a prosperous royal town with ten monasteries and thousands of monks.

Singara-Iraq.name: Singara
Singara-Iraq.evidence_basis: Roman legionary colony of Legio I Parthica (~55 ha fortified town below Jebel Sinjar; Oates 1968), captured and depopulated by Shapur II in 360 AD before continuing as a smaller Sassanian frontier town.

Yazd-Iran.name: Yazd
Yazd-Iran.evidence_basis: Central plateau qanat-irrigated oasis and Zoroastrian stronghold (~55 ha; Bonine 1980; Brunner 1983), expanded under Yazdegerd I as a fortified caravan station linking Fars, Kirman, and Rayy.

Thaj-Saudi Arabia.name: Thaj
Thaj-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Largest pre-Islamic Hellenistic-Parthian city in Eastern Arabia (~40 ha ashlar stone-walled urban center plus extensive suburbs; Potts 1990; Rohmer et al. 2018; Farrokh 2023), widely linked to classical Gerrha.

Volubilis-Morocco.name: Volubilis
Volubilis-Morocco.evidence_basis: Mauretanian-Roman inland oil-producing municipium (~42 ha walled circuit; Lenoir 1985; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016 ~14k-19k) continuing as a post-Roman Christian/Berber town after the 285 AD Roman administrative withdrawal.

Syene-Egypt.name: Syene
Syene-Egypt.evidence_basis: First Cataract frontier garrison, customs post, and granite-quarrying center opposite Elephantine (~38 ha; Pilgrim et al. 2008; Tacoma 2006), housing three Roman cohorts and late antique border troops.

Qaryat al-Faw-Saudi Arabia.name: Qaryat al-Faw
Qaryat al-Faw-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Capital of the first Kingdom of Kindah along the Wadi al-Dawasir trade corridor (~60 ha dense suq, palace, and residential core within irrigated oasis; Al-Ansary 1982), declining sharply in the 4th-5th c. AD.

Amathus-Cyprus.name: Amathus
Amathus-Cyprus.evidence_basis: Ancient Eteocypriot kingdom and Roman district capital (~40 ha enclosed acropolis and lower harbor town; Aupert 1996; Hanson 2016) with prosperous Late Antique basilicas.

Thamugadi-Algeria.name: Thamugadi
Thamugadi-Algeria.evidence_basis: Veteran colony founded 100 AD by Trajan on a 12 ha grid expanding to ~50 ha with extramural quarters (Courtois 1951; Wilson 2011; Hanson 2016 ~12k-16k), sacked by Aures tribes c. 484 AD and partially refortified by Solomon in 539 AD.

Kourion-Cyprus.name: Kourion
Kourion-Cyprus.evidence_basis: South-coast limestone promontory polis (~40 ha acropolis and lower town plus stadium; Swiny 1982; Hanson 2016) devastated by the 365 AD earthquake and partially rebuilt as an early Christian bishopric.

Sohar-Oman.name: Sohar
Sohar-Oman.evidence_basis: Batinah coastal copper-exporting and Indian Ocean trading port (~40 ha late pre-Islamic/Sassanian Mazun urban precursor; Williamson 1973; Kervran 2004), expanding under Sassanian Gulf commerce.

Dura-Europos-Syria.name: Dura-Europos
Dura-Europos-Syria.evidence_basis: Seleucid-Parthian-Roman Euphrates fortress-town (~52-70 ha walled plateau with dense excavated insulae; Hopkins 1979; Baird 2018; Farrokh 2023), destroyed and permanently abandoned after Shapur I's 256 AD siege.

Tayma-Saudi Arabia.name: Tayma
Tayma-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Ancient fortified Hijazi-Nefud oasis (~950 ha outer defensive wall enclosing ~45 ha residential core and Bir Haddaj oasis; Eichmann et al. 2006-2016), former residence of Nabonidus and enduring caravan junction.

Bulla Regia-Tunisia.name: Bulla Regia
Bulla Regia-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Former Numidian royal residence and Hadrianic colonia in the fertile Medjerda valley (~60 ha; Beschaouch et al. 1977; Hanson 2016) noted for subterranean peristyle villas and imperial baths.

Siraf-Iran.name: Siraf
Siraf-Iran.evidence_basis: Sassanid naval fort and nascent Indian Ocean maritime emporium excavated beneath the Islamic Friday mosque (~35 ha late Sassanid coastal sector; Whitehouse 1974/2009), serving Firuzabad's overseas trade.

Phasis-Georgia.name: Phasis
Phasis-Georgia.evidence_basis: Milesian Greek colony and Roman Black Sea garrison port at the Rioni delta (Strabo 11.2.17; Braund 1994; Lordkipanidze 2000), famous for its 4th c. AD rhetorical academy and Lazic maritime commerce.

Hegra-Saudi Arabia.name: Hegra
Hegra-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Southernmost major Nabataean city and Roman auxiliary frontier post (~50 ha walled mudbrick urban core surrounded by 111 monumental rock-cut tombs; Nehmé et al. 2010-2018), contracting after 3rd c. overland trade decline.

Dioscurias-Georgia.name: Dioscurias
Dioscurias-Georgia.evidence_basis: Milesian trade emporium rebuilt as the Roman Pontic limes fortress Sebastopolis (Arrian Periplus; Braund 1994), serving as the chief coastal market for northwestern Caucasian highland tribes.

Qal'at al-Bahrain-Bahrain.name: Qal'at al-Bahrain
Qal'at al-Bahrain-Bahrain.evidence_basis: Tylos pearl-diving and maritime entrepot (~35 ha tell and oasis hinterland with late Parthian-Sassanian coastal fortress; Højlund 2006; Potts 1990; Farrokh 2023).

Thugga-Tunisia.name: Thugga
Thugga-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Numidian hilltop town and Roman colonia (~65 ha sprawling terraced hillside with 3,500-seat theater; Khanoussi & Maurin 2000; Hanson 2016), assessed at ~10k-12k peak inhabitants.

Mecca-Saudi Arabia.name: Mecca
Mecca-Saudi Arabia.evidence_basis: Sanctuary and Quraysh caravan trading town consolidated in the 5th-6th c. AD in an arid Hijazi valley (Watt 1953; Donner 1981; Crone 1987), assessed at ~6k-12k permanent residents by the early 7th century.

Archaeopolis-Georgia.name: Archaeopolis
Archaeopolis-Georgia.evidence_basis: Fortified royal capital of Lazica/Egrisi on the Tekhuri River (~20 ha triple-walled citadel and lower town plus extramural villages; Everill et al. 2014), heavily contested during the 6th c. Byzantine-Sassanian Lazic Wars.

Qana-Yemen.name: Qana
Qana-Yemen.evidence_basis: Principal Hadrami frankincense port recorded in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (~35 ha excavated harbor town and warehouses; Sedov 1992/2007), linking Indian Ocean and Mediterranean maritime trade.

Surkh Kotal-Afghanistan.name: Surkh Kotal
Surkh Kotal-Afghanistan.evidence_basis: Kushan dynastic sanctuary and Baghlan valley settlement founded under Kanishka I (~35 ha sanctuary acropolis and valley town; Schlumberger 1983), contracting after the mid-3rd c. fire destruction of the temple.

Sala Colonia-Morocco.name: Sala Colonia
Sala Colonia-Morocco.evidence_basis: Southernmost Atlantic Roman municipium and military limes outpost on the Bou Regreg (~35 ha; Boube 1999; Hanson 2016).

Berenike-Egypt.name: Berenike
Berenike-Egypt.evidence_basis: Founded c. 275 BC by Ptolemy II as a Red Sea elephant-transport and Indo-Roman spice emporium (~35 ha excavated town; Sidebotham 2011), peaking in the 1st c. AD and 4th-5th c. revival before mid-6th c. abandonment.

Myos Hormos-Egypt.name: Myos Hormos
Myos Hormos-Egypt.evidence_basis: Ptolemaic-Roman Red Sea harbor (~22 ha excavated port and lagoon quay; Peacock & Blue 2006; Sidebotham 2011) handling up to 120 India-bound ships annually under Augustus (Strabo 2.5.12) before silting and 3rd c. AD abandonment.

Sumhuram-Oman.name: Sumhuram
Sumhuram-Oman.evidence_basis: Fortified Hadrami frankincense port in Dhofar (~1 ha fortified stone acropolis plus extramural lagoon port quarters; Avanzini 2002-2015), exporting Dhofari resin to Qana and India before 5th c. AD abandonment.
